newsitem.title: KENYA: Freed American arrives in Kenya from Somalia.
newsitem.headline: Freed American arrives in Kenya from Somalia.

text.p: An American aid worker freed by Somali kidnappers arrived in Kenya from Mogadishu on Wednesday and a Somali faction leader said his abduction was a result of mistaken identity.
"I'm tired, I'm going to go to sleep," Daniel Suther told Reuters on arrival at Nairobi's international airport on a U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) plane from north Mogadishu.
Suther, who said he was a former journalist from near San Francisco refused to say what had happened to him in Somalia, where he was kidnapped by at least eight gunmen on Tuesday.
U.S. embassy officials were waiting for him as he left the plane in Nairobi and met with him for almost an hour before he emerged through the airport arrivals gate, looking pale and shaking.
Suther, who was working on contract for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) was freed earlier on Wednesday in the town of Giohar, 70 km (43 miles) north of the capital.
He was abducted in north Mogadishu shortly after meeting faction leader Ali Mahdi Mohammed and on his release he was driven back there and spoke to reporters at Ali Mahdi's office.
"I am safe and healthy except I am dirty and tired," said Suther, who USAID officials said was on a mission with other aid workers to check on the food situation in north Mogadishu.
Ali Mahdi said the kidnappers were hired by a group of businessmen who said WFP owed them money. He said Suther was seized because they wrongly that thought he worked for WFP.
On Tuesday, the gunmen disarmed Suther's two Somali guards and drove off with him and his Somali driver heading north.
They said Ali Mahdi, whose Abgal clan alliance controls north Mogadishu, ordered the arrest of the kidnappers and sent two "technicals", four-wheel-drive battlewagons, after him.

Kidnappings and extortion, especially involving staff of foreign aid agencies, are common in Mogadishu, where weapons are easily available and unemployment has run high since the departure of the U.N. peacekeeping operation in March 1995.
International aid agencies pulled all foreign staff out of southern Mogadishu, controlled by forces loyal to faction leader Hussein Aideed, earlier this year, but kept some staff in north Mogadishu.
The northern part of the divided and war-scarred city was widely considered less dangerous than the south for foreigners.

Somali gunmen have abducted more than 20 aid workers in the last three years in disputes over money. All were freed after negotiations but several foreigners were killed in other incidents. Somalia has had no central government or authority since the fall of late dictator Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991.

The south Mogadishu-based faction led by Hussein Aideed said last Friday it would free within days a 25-year-old Australian pilot sentenced to 25 years in prison for making a forced landing in western Somalia in May.
